title: HIPAA Readiness Assessment
disclaimer: This is a readiness checklist for internal planning. It is not legal advice, a HIPAA certification, or a guarantee of compliance.
phi_warning: Do not enter patient names, medical details, or any other PHI. Use practice names and vendor names only.

sections.title: Privacy Rule
sections.blurb: How the practice notices patients, limits uses of PHI, and honors patient rights.

questions.text: Patients receive a Notice of Privacy Practices, and a current copy is posted where people can see it.
questions.help: HIPAA requires a NPP at first service and a posted copy. Keep a signed acknowledgment or document a good-faith attempt.

questions.text: Staff only access the minimum PHI needed for their job (role-based access, not 'everyone sees everything').
questions.help: Shared logins and open charts on every workstation are common gaps.

questions.text: A written authorization is collected before using PHI for marketing or other non-treatment purposes.
questions.help: Treatment, payment, and health-care operations usually do not need extra authorization. Marketing and most sale of PHI do.

questions.text: There is a written process to give patients a copy of their records within the required time (typically 30 days).
questions.help: Delays and 'we don't release records' policies are frequent complaint triggers.

questions.text: Patients can request amendments and an accounting of certain disclosures, and staff know how to handle that.
questions.help: You do not have to agree to every amendment, but you do need a documented process and response.

sections.title: Administrative safeguards
sections.blurb: Named owners, written policies, risk analysis, training, and a backup plan.

questions.text: A named security official (and privacy official, if different) is responsible for HIPAA.
questions.help: In a small practice this can be the owner plus a manager — but someone has to own it in writing.

questions.text: Written HIPAA privacy and security policies exist and staff can find them.
questions.help: Verbal rules only will not hold up in an investigation.

questions.text: A security risk analysis has been completed in the last 12 months and is written down.
questions.help: OCR almost always asks for this. A one-page inventory of systems + threats + current controls is a start.

questions.text: Open risks have owners, due dates, and a follow-up review.
questions.help: Finding gaps without fixing them is still a finding.

questions.text: New hires get HIPAA training before handling PHI, and the whole team trains at least annually, with attendance logged.
questions.help: Keep dated sign-in sheets or LMS records. Include front desk, providers, and anyone who can see the schedule.

questions.text: There is a written sanction policy for workforce HIPAA violations, and it is applied consistently.
questions.help: Covers snooping in charts, sharing passwords, and texting PHI on personal phones.

questions.text: There is a contingency plan: backups, how to restore, and how to operate if systems are down.
questions.help: Include ransomware and a lost/stolen laptop scenario.

questions.text: Security measures are reviewed at least yearly or after a major system change.
questions.help: New EHR, new billing vendor, or a move to a new office should trigger a review.

sections.title: Physical safeguards
sections.blurb: Who can walk in, what screens show, and how devices are stored or destroyed.

questions.text: Only authorized people can reach areas and rooms where PHI is stored or discussed.
questions.help: Locked records room, badge or key control, and a visitor process.

questions.text: Workstations and waiting-area screens are positioned so visitors cannot read PHI.
questions.help: Privacy screens and turning monitors away from the lobby count.

questions.text: Unattended computers lock automatically and staff lock when they step away.
questions.help: Five minutes or less is a practical default for front-desk machines.

questions.text: There is an inventory of laptops, phones, USBs, and servers that can store ePHI.
questions.help: You cannot protect what you have not listed.

questions.text: Paper PHI is shredded and electronic media is wiped or destroyed before reuse or disposal.
questions.help: Old hard drives in a closet and dumpster charts are classic failures.

sections.title: Technical safeguards
sections.blurb: Unique logins, encryption, logs, and access that ends when someone leaves.

questions.text: Every user has a unique login. Shared EHR or email passwords are not used.
questions.help: Shared 'front desk' accounts make it impossible to know who accessed a chart.

questions.text: MFA is on for email, EHR, and remote access. Passwords are not reused or written on sticky notes.
questions.help: Email is often how attackers reach ePHI even when the EHR is stronger.

questions.text: EHR and workstations auto-logoff after inactivity.
questions.help: Required under technical safeguards as an addressable access-control method. Use it unless you have a documented alternative.

questions.text: Devices and backups that hold ePHI are encrypted at rest.
questions.help: Full-disk encryption on laptops plus encrypted backups. A stolen unencrypted laptop is a reportable incident.

questions.text: ePHI is sent only over encrypted channels (HTTPS, TLS email, secure portal) — not open SMS or personal email.
questions.help: Texting photos of charts on iMessage/WhatsApp is a common small-practice gap.

questions.text: Access logs exist for the EHR (and key systems) and someone reviews them on a schedule.
questions.help: Even a monthly spot-check for snooping is better than never looking.

questions.text: Access is removed the same day a staff member or contractor leaves.
questions.help: Include EHR, email, cloud drives, and the alarm code.

questions.text: Workstations have current OS updates and malware protection.
questions.help: Unpatched Windows boxes at the front desk are a frequent ransomware entry.

sections.title: Business associates
sections.blurb: Anyone outside the practice who can see PHI needs a signed BAA.

questions.text: There is a current list of every vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI.
questions.help: EHR, billing, IT, cloud backup, email, SMS, answering service, shredding, and website forms if they collect health info.

questions.text: A signed Business Associate Agreement is on file for each of those vendors.
questions.help: A vendor Terms of Service is not a BAA. Use the BAA register in this tool to track them.

questions.text: BAAs are reviewed when a vendor is added, changed, or dropped.
questions.help: Switching billing companies or adding an AI scribe is a trigger.

questions.text: BAAs require vendors to flow HIPAA duties down to their subcontractors.
questions.help: Standard in a proper BAA template. Confirm it is actually in the signed copy.

sections.title: Breach notification
sections.blurb: What happens in the first 24 hours if PHI is lost, stolen, or exposed.

questions.text: There is a written incident / breach response plan with who to call first.
questions.help: Owner, privacy official, IT, and counsel. Include after-hours contacts.

questions.text: Staff know to run a four-factor breach risk assessment before deciding it is 'not a breach.'
questions.help: Nature of PHI, who received it, whether it was actually viewed, and mitigation. Document the decision either way.

questions.text: The team knows the clock: notify affected people and HHS without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery (sooner for large breaches).
questions.help: 500+ individuals has extra media / HHS timing rules. State AG rules may be faster — check counsel.

questions.text: Lost phone / stolen laptop / misdirected email has been walked through at least once this year.
questions.help: A 15-minute tabletop counts. Write down what you would actually do.
